_meta: A Gaussian blur's standard deviation and a set of truncation radii, used to show why a Gaussian kernel must be sized to its sigma -- radius about three sigma -- and why a radius chosen too small drops a real fraction of the kernel's weight. A Gaussian never reaches zero; it has infinite tails, so any finite kernel is a truncated Gaussian, and the sampled weights inside the radius sum to less than the full integral. How much less depends entirely on the radius measured in sigmas: a radius of one sigma captures only the central bump and leaves a large fraction of the weight in the discarded tails, while three sigma captures about 99.7 percent. Two consequences follow. First, if the truncated kernel is applied without renormalizing, it sums to less than one, so it scales every pixel down -- the whole image darkens by the missing weight fraction (this is different from a border darkening, which affects only the edges; here the interior darkens too). Second, even if the kernel is renormalized to sum to one so brightness is restored, a too-small radius still produces a narrower blur than requested, because chopping off the tails removes the far neighbors that a wide Gaussian is supposed to mix in -- the effective standard deviation of the truncated kernel is smaller than the sigma you asked for. The fix is to size the radius to the sigma, conventionally ceil(3*sigma), and renormalize. sigma is the Gaussian's standard deviation in pixels; radii is the list of truncation radii (in pixels) to compare. These are the fixture; the captured weight fraction, the unnormalized brightness, and the effective variance at each radius are computed.
